clue.text: The very thing I do?

parts.note: read the question as the Roman numeral I followed by 'do', short for ditto: a single figure and then a repeat of it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a thing is exactly what they themselves do.
explanation.walkthrough: I is the Roman numeral for one, and 'do' is the old written short form of ditto. So 'I do' reads as one figure followed by a mark meaning the same again.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom stressing identity, as when two apparently different things turn out to be identical.

clue.text: Don't worry, if some reported missing?

definitions.meaning: a casual reassurance that everything is fine
'some' sounds like 'sum', and a maths sum is a problem, so with the sums missing there would be none of them

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off the news that a few things have gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading turns on 'some' sounding like 'sum', and a sum being an arithmetic problem: take the sums away and there are none left to set.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an everyday idiom of reassurance telling someone a matter causes no difficulty.

clue.text: Oh no, that's horrible as Hagar

indicators.note: something horrible is a mess, so the name beside it is jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: An exclamation of dismay compared to Hagar the Horrible, the Viking of the comic strip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horrible' borrows the title of the Hagar the Horrible comic strip but signals rearranging the five letters of Hagar.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are interjections of frustration or dismay, the longer one a cartoon-style cry of exasperation.

clue.text: Made in the mould of a Conservative rising at beginning of speech in parliament

indicators.note: in places the turned pair and the extra letter inside the word for the assembly

parts.note: a diet is a legislative assembly, as in the Japanese or historic German parliaments

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the words a and Conservative are read upwards
the beginning of a word is its first letter, here taken from speech

explanation.surface: A Tory politician stands to make a maiden speech in the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns A C into CA in this down clue; 'beginning of' gives S; 'in' puts CAS inside DIET, a word for a national assembly.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal objects that are die-cast are formed by pouring molten metal into a mould.

clue.text: Tricky place to put sexy bottom

parts.note: hot is slang for sexually attractive
a seat is a person's backside

explanation.surface: Advice on where an attractive behind might be awkwardly positioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in this position, as on a quiz show or under questioning, means facing awkward pressure and difficult scrutiny.

clue.text: … includes a short new blog about red light area?

indicators.note: includes means the number named by the clue's own label holds the shuffled letters

parts.note: the ellipsis carries on from the clue's own number, 6, read as the word six

indicators.note: about signals the letters being turned around and rearranged

parts.note: N is the usual abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A blogger writes briefly about a district known for vice.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis makes the clue's own number, 6, its opening word. The rearranged letters spell GNALBO.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway cabin from which signals are worked, including the red lights that stop trains: a cheeky redefinition of a sleazy district.

clue.text: Quiet time, briefly, before playing duet

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for minute, a unit of time

indicators.note: playing suggests the duet being performed in a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A short pause before two musicians perform their duet.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: something softened or silenced is subdued in sound.

clue.text: Badminton, say, for the long weekend?

definitions.meaning: Badminton Horse Trials is an equestrian competition held over several days, not the racquet sport
a weekend with an extra day off is an occasion spanning that many days

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a game of shuttlecock fills a bank holiday weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: Badminton is an English country estate that hosts a famous horse-trials competition, not the racquet game the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse trials of dressage, cross-country and showjumping are this kind of competition; a bank holiday weekend lasts the same span.

clue.text: Boundary sign on border out here, perhaps

parts.note: in cricket a ball reaching the boundary along the ground scores four runs
a poster is a printed notice or sign
a flower border in a garden is a bed

explanation.surface: A notice about a boundary placed on the edge of a field.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a ball that crosses the boundary after touching the ground scores four runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sound asleep is 'out', and a grand canopied bed is where that might happen.

clue.text: What links husband with awfully pretty ex

indicators.note: awfully signals the letters being badly jumbled

explanation.surface: A wife's new partner compared unflatteringly with her very attractive former spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Web text is built from clickable connections that join one page to another.

clue.text: Reach deprived area with no hospital

indicators.note: with no means the hospital letter is taken away

parts.note: a ghetto is a poor, run-down part of a city
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Getting to a poor district that lacks a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means arrive at or get as far as, a synonym for reach.

clue.text: What about political correctness around "old age"?

indicators.note: about puts the outer exclamation round everything else

parts.note: eh is an exclamation asking someone to repeat themselves

indicators.note: around places the abbreviation for correctness either side of the old letter

parts.note: PC is the common abbreviation for politically correct

explanation.surface: A question about whether the phrase 'old age' is still acceptable language.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'old age' look like one phrase, but 'old' is wordplay and only 'age' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: an era or period of history, like an age.

clue.text: A regular swimmer's taken by to see the old king

indicators.note: taken means the swimmer's name holds the multiplication letter

parts.note: in Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont every night to visit Hero
X is the multiplication sign, as in three by four

explanation.surface: A frequent swimmer is taken somewhere to visit an ancient monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to see Hero, hence 'regular swimmer'. 'by' is X as in 3 by 4.
explanation.definitionFit: Several kings bore this name, notably the Macedonian conqueror called the Great and three medieval Scottish rulers.

clue.text: Least exciting airport to start from

parts.note: Dulles is the international airport serving Washington DC

indicators.note: the start of the word to is its first letter

explanation.surface: A traveller rates the dullest airport to fly out of.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of dull, meaning most boring or least interesting.

clue.text: Exam initially chosen for a type of college in the US

definitions.text: a type of college in the US

indicators.note: initially means the word for chosen comes first, before the exam

parts.note: elect means chosen, as in president-elect
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: An entrance test for an American college, reported as chosen first.
explanation.definitionFit: The body of electors that formally picks the American president is called the Electoral College, so the word describes that kind of college.

clue.text: Commander and navigator retired for shag?

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn, so the explorer's name goes backwards

parts.note: John Cabot was the explorer who sailed to North America in 1497
CO stands for commanding officer

explanation.surface: A naval officer and his navigator go to bed together.
explanation.walkthrough: Shag is a coarse-cut tobacco, but in British slang the word also means sex, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Shag is a strong coarsely shredded pipe smoke, an example of the leaf it names.

clue.text: Lament about surprisingly barren bush

indicators.note: about places the cry around the shuffled letters

parts.note: to lament is to weep or cry

indicators.note: surprisingly means the letters of barren come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Someone weeps over a shrub that has unexpectedly borne no fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant is a low shrub bearing tart red berries, so it is an example of a bush.

clue.text: Complains noisily, if sweet potato gets immersed after two peelings

parts.note: a yam is a starchy tuber often called a sweet potato

indicators.note: peeling twice strips two layers off each end of the word immersed

explanation.surface: Grumbling over a potato dunked in water after peeling it twice.
explanation.walkthrough: One peeling takes the first and last letters off; a second peeling does it again.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to keep on loudly whining and grumbling.

clue.text: It's key to adult having fun around Hull or Grimsby, say

indicators.note: around means the word for fun goes round the two letters

parts.note: sport means fun or amusement
E is a musical key
A is the film-classification abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: An adult enjoying themselves in two English towns on the Humber.
explanation.definitionFit: Hull and Grimsby are harbour towns on the Humber estuary in northern England, examples of towns with docks.

clue.text: How's your father to beat time as part of a circle?

parts.note: British slang, comically coy, for sexual activity
to tan someone's hide is to beat them

explanation.surface: A child asks after a father and is told to watch the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How's your father' is a jokey British euphemism for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a sixth of a full round, sixty degrees, which the navigation instrument's arc spans.

clue.text: Battered plaice's a dish not on the menu

definitions.text: a dish not on the menu

indicators.note: battered means knocked about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fish in batter offered as an off-menu dish of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' looks like cooking but signals rearranging the letters of PLAICES.
explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant's special is a dish offered on the day apart from the printed list.

clue.text: 9 ate out after 6 in Asian capital

indicators.note: after means the shuffled letters follow the Roman numeral

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of order

parts.note: the figure is spelt out as a word

explanation.surface: Someone eats at nine o'clock after six in an Asian city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes the old joke 'seven ate nine'; 'out' rearranges NINE and ATE into ENTIANE.
explanation.definitionFit: The city on the Mekong is the seat of government of Laos.

clue.text: Leave from 19 down

indicators.note: from means the answer is drawn out of the spelt-out words, leaving their outer letters behind

parts.note: the figure written out as a word
taken as written, spelt out

explanation.surface: An instruction that seems to send the solver to another clue for the meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: '19 down' looks like a cross-reference to SEAPORT, but the words are to be spelt out: the answer sits within 'nineteen down', with NINETE in front and N after dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave in a will is to bequeath, providing funds or property for someone.

clue.text: Exclude being served by rude baristas

indicators.note: the answer is served up inside the phrase that follows, its letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: Refusing to be waited on by impolite coffee-shop staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to bar or prohibit someone from something.

clue.text: Dead small and born a fool

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small
B is the abbreviation for born, as in biographies

explanation.surface: A tiny, foolish creature that came into the world lifeless.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a boring, socially inept person, roughly a nerd or dope.

clue.text: Darn it! Whipping time — poor bottom!

indicators.note: poor signals a bad arrangement of the letters
whipping means stealing, so the time letter is taken away

explanation.surface: A cry of pain at a caning that leaves a sore behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whipping' means stealing: take T from IT to leave I. Then 'poor' rearranges DARN and I to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: the lowest point of anything.

clue.text: Source of peace symbol appearing as repeated note by tenor in musical

indicators.note: in puts the tenor letter inside the musical's title

parts.note: Oliver! is Lionel Bart's musical based on Oliver Twist

indicators.note: repeated means the note letter appears twice

parts.note: E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A tenor in a musical sings the same note twice in a peace number.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver! is Lionel Bart's stage musical of Oliver Twist; 'by' just sets the doubled note beside the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The olive branch, emblem of peace, comes from this Mediterranean plant.

clue.text: Those keeping note of regnal number?

definitions.text: Those keeping note of regnal number?

parts.words: Those keeping note of regnal number
parts.note: a monarch's regnal number II is a pair of small strokes, two tiny letter i's, read here as a pair of youngsters

explanation.walkthrough: The regnal II (as in Elizabeth II) is two small i's side by side, like a pair of young lads; the phrase is also the title of Rolf Harris's 1969 chart-topping song.
explanation.definitionFit: A whimsical cryptic description: the pair of tiny figures in a monarch's numeral are pictured as youngsters.
